priority.override_reason: Ranks 1 through 26 are closed for this cycle by exact-current retained, rejected, or explicitly skipped frame, constructor, object, string, RegExp, typed-loop, dense-loop, and Number-only evidence. Fresh exact-current profiles of ranks 27 through 30 isolate one distinct low-cost mechanism at rank 27: functional RegExp replacement copies the complete immutable subject into a new Rust String before every callback even though the runtime already represents the same JavaScript string with a shared JsString allocation. The copy consumes 3,100 of 9,431 samples by itself. Rank 28 is distributed generic VM and Value ownership cost, rank 29 reproduces already-consumed RegExp matcher families, and rank 30 reproduces the retained typed-loop executor plus distributed array/property costs. Although the new cost dominates only one freshly profiled workload, its 32.9% directly removable share, exact shared representation, and semantic locality justify a one-attempt rank-27 override rather than beginning another structural matcher or execution-tier campaign.

mechanism.summary: Keep the replace subject as the runtime's shared immutable JsString through result construction and pass a cheap clone of that shared handle as the functional replacer's input argument, instead of converting the subject to an owned Rust String and cloning the complete buffer once per match.
mechanism.generality: The mechanism applies to every String.prototype.replace or RegExp.prototype[Symbol.replace] call that reaches the ordinary builtin functional-replacement path, independent of pattern source, flags, subject length, replacement callback identity, match count, or benchmark. Result assembly continues to borrow the identical subject text and uses the existing UTF-16 slicing and string-length checks. Each callback still receives a primitive string with exactly the original subject contents; only its unobservable immutable backing allocation is shared. String-replacement paths, custom exec methods, subclass/prototype observability, capture materialization, match order, lastIndex behavior, and result allocation remain unchanged. No source text, benchmark name, input size, iteration count, checksum, or expected output participates.
semantic_risks: passing the original complete subject to every callback in the same argument position even when earlier callbacks mutate unrelated objects or RegExp state
preserving primitive-string value semantics while sharing only the runtime's immutable backing allocation
keeping UTF-16 match positions, unmatched slices, substitution slices, maximum string length checks, and callback result coercion unchanged
not extending the optimization to observable custom exec or replacement protocols beyond the existing builtin dispatch boundary
retaining the subject for the full replace operation without creating a reference cycle or permitting in-place mutation through JsString copy-on-write

profile_evidence.shared_cost: Of 9,431 main-thread samples, 7,877 are inside String.prototype.replace and 3,313 reach native_regexp_prototype_replace at the call site that clones the subject for the functional replacer. Rust String::clone accounts for 3,102 inclusive samples there, including 3,100 samples in platform memmove. The direct full-buffer copy is therefore 32.87% of the whole profile before counting allocation and deallocation. JsString already documents clone as a shared reference-count bump and immutable JavaScript string values make the backing identity unobservable, so this is a redundant representation conversion rather than required matcher or callback work.
